svg.title: A nurse caring for a patient receiving TPN through a central line meets resistance when attempting to flush and notes the infusion has become sluggish; the external catheter length appears longer than documented. What should the nurse do?
svg.desc: SUSPECTED OCCLUSION, THROMBOSIS, OR CATHETER MIGRATION IS THE ONE SITUATION WHERE THE NURSE STOPS A TPN INFUSION WITHOUT WAITING FOR A PROVIDER ORDER, because this risk outweighs the risk of rebound hypoglycemia. Do NOT force a flush — the central line tip sits at the heart, so popping a clot loose sends it straight there, and forcing air or a displaced catheter risks an air embolism. Continuing or speeding up the infusion into a migrated or occluded line pushes concentrated TPN into the wrong space and delays recognition. Stop the infusion, inspect the catheter, and notify the provider.
